abstract: Cortical gamma oscillations often arrive in bursts locked to the phase of slower theta waves, a pattern called theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC). PAC is linked to memory and altered in epilepsy, but most models tie it to particular cells or circuits. We start from a generalized Langevin equation, an equation of motion for a few collective variables in which friction and random forces stand for the unobserved neural activity, and let its stiffness and friction depend on the state. Expanding them to first order in the theta and gamma variables yields ten possible interaction terms; only the two friction type terms change gamma energy and produce PAC, and depending on the term and its sign the gamma bursts sit at the peak, trough, rising or falling phase of theta. We study a gamma friction that follows theta velocity as a simplified example. Because the time integral of theta velocity is theta coordinate, the gamma amplitude rises and falls with theta coordinate as exp(gvvx{theta}/2). The fluctuation dissipation theorem turns noise and damping into a theta effective temperature, and the PAC strength becomes a closed form function of one dimensionless number, kappa , that combines the coupling with this temperature. Without fitted parameters, this prediction accounts for 51,095 simulated records (R2 = 0.993) and for the median PAC of 5,160 combinations of coupling and damping (R2 = 0.989). The coupling also drives gamma out of equilibrium: its kinetic temperature grows far above the one inferred from its response. All coefficients enter linearly so that they can, in principle, be estimated from recordings by linear regression. A companion paper shows that the same number sets the distance to a stability boundary.
